title: A novel anticancer natural product SP09 selectively targets KRAS-mutant NSCLC through LKB1/AMPK/mTOR modulation: implications for novel therapeutic development
author: Peng Yue; Chitin Hon; Xiaoping Zhao; Fayaz Ali; Jiayi Sun; Jiyou Kou
text:
Abstract
KRAS-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a major therapeutic challenge due to the paucity of effective targeted agents. Although covalent KRAS^G12C inhibitorsi such as sotorasib and adagrasib have demonstrated clinical activity, pooled analyses indicate only modest response rates and short progression-free survival, with no effective options for non-G12C subtypes. This highlights the need for novel therapeutic strategies with broader efficacy and improved durability. We evaluated the antiproliferative effects of SP09, a novel benzoin-Schiff base derivative, in KRAS-mutant (A549, H460) and EGFR-mutant (PC9) NSCLC cells, as well as normal lung cells. Cell viability, colony formation, and cell cycle distribution were assessed, and the involvement of the liver kinase B1 (LKB1)/AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK)/mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling axis was examined by western blot. SP09 selectively inhibited the proliferation of KRAS-mutant NSCLC cells (IC50 ≈ 29 µM) with minimal toxicity to normal lung cells. Treatment induced G2/M arrest via downregulation of cyclin B1 and upregulation of p21. Mechanistically, SP09 activated the LKB1/AMPK pathway and suppressed mTOR signaling, leading to inhibition of downstream effectors, including P70S6K, S6, and sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1 (SREBP1). SP09 exerts potent and selective antiproliferative effects in KRAS-mutant NSCLC through dual regulation of cell cycle and metabolic signaling pathways. Given the restricted efficacy and rapid resistance associated with current KRAS-targeted therapies, our data highlight SP09 as a promising candidate for further preclinical development with potential translational value in KRAS-driven NSCLC.
Keywords: anticancer drug, KRAS mutation, LKB1/AMPK/mTOR pathway, natural products, nonsmall cell lung cancer
Introduction
Lung cancer continues to rank as the foremost cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, with an estimated 2.2 million new cases and 1.8 million deaths reported in 2025 [1]. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for approximately 85% of these cases. It is often diagnosed at an advanced stage, resulting in a 5-year survival rate that remains dismally low despite substantial progress in diagnostic and therapeutic strategies [2]. In China, the incidence and mortality of NSCLC have been steadily increasing, largely due to persistent exposure to tobacco smoke, air pollution, and occupational carcinogens, imposing an enormous health and economic burden on society [2–4]. These realities underscore the urgent need for more effective therapeutic options, particularly for patients who do not benefit from currently available targeted therapies. Over the past two decades, the treatment landscape of NSCLC has been transformed by the advent of molecularly targeted therapies. Agents such as osimertinib for Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutated tumors and alectinib for ALK-rearranged disease have delivered remarkable survival benefits, setting new standards for precision oncology [5,6]. However, kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homolog (KRAS) mutations—among the most prevalent oncogenic drivers in NSCLC—have long been deemed ‘undruggable’ because of their high affinity for guanosine triphosphate (GTP)/guanosine diphosphate (GDP) and lack of deep binding pockets suitable for small-molecule inhibitors [7]. KRAS mutations occur in roughly 25–30% of lung adenocarcinomas in Western populations and 10–15% in Asian cohorts, with KRAS G12C, KRAS G12D, and KRAS G12V representing the most frequent subtypes [7–9]. These alterations are often associated with primary resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors and with poorer clinical outcomes, making them a formidable challenge in NSCLC management.
Recent years have witnessed the development of covalent KRAS^G12C inhibitors, including sotorasib and adagrasib, which exploit a previously hidden allosteric pocket to selectively target the mutant cysteine residue [10–12]. While these agents have yielded promising clinical responses, their efficacy is limited to the G12C subtype, which represents only a fraction of KRAS mutations. Moreover, resistance frequently emerges via secondary KRAS mutations, amplification, or activation of bypass signaling pathways such as phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/protein kinase B (AKT) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascade [13,14]. Consequently, there remains a pressing unmet need for therapeutic strategies capable of targeting a broader spectrum of KRAS mutations and overcoming adaptive resistance mechanisms.
Natural products and their synthetic derivatives have historically served as indispensable resources in anticancer drug discovery, accounting for more than 60% of currently approved chemotherapeutic agents [15,16]. These compounds offer unparalleled structural diversity and biological activity, frequently enabling the simultaneous modulation of multiple molecular targets involved in tumorigenesis [17]. Such multitarget potential is particularly advantageous for malignancies like KRAS-mutant NSCLC, where tumor heterogeneity and signaling network plasticity render single-pathway inhibition insufficient for durable responses [18]. For instance, several plant-derived alkaloids and flavonoids have been shown to attenuate KRAS-driven oncogenic signaling by interfering with downstream effectors such as the rapidly accelerated fibrosarcoma (RAF)–mitogen-activated protein kinase (MEK)–extracellular signal–regulated kinase (ERK) and PI3K–AKT–mTOR pathways [19,20]. Moreover, natural product scaffolds often provide favorable physicochemical properties for further medicinal chemistry optimization, facilitating the generation of derivatives with improved potency, selectivity, and pharmacokinetic profiles [21]. Despite these advantages, relatively few studies have systematically explored natural product-inspired compounds for the treatment of KRAS-mutant lung cancer, underscoring an untapped opportunity in drug development.
In this context, we focused on SP09, a synthetic benzoin-derived Schiff base formally named (E)-N′-(2-hydroxy-1,2-diphenylethylidene) benzohydrazide, as a potential therapeutic candidate for KRAS-mutant NSCLC. Benzoin derivatives have been reported to possess diverse pharmacological properties, and the Schiff base moiety confers structural flexibility for further optimization of biological activity. The synthetic route of SP09 (Fig. 1a) involves the condensation of benzohydrazide with benzoin under controlled conditions, yielding a crystalline compound with high purity. Structural elucidation was confirmed through 1H-nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and 13C-NMR spectroscopy, as well as high-resolution mass spectrometry, which collectively verified the expected molecular framework (Fig. 1b). The chemical structure of SP09, featuring a central C=N imine linkage and hydroxyl-substituted diphenylethylidene group, is illustrated in Figure 1c. This scaffold design was intended to enhance lipophilicity, facilitate cellular uptake, and enable interaction with key molecular targets involved in tumor cell proliferation.
Our preliminary biological screening revealed that SP09 exhibited potent cytotoxic activity against KRAS-mutant NSCLC cell lines (A549 and H460) and EGFR-mutant PC9 cells, while exerting minimal effects on normal human lung epithelial Bronchial epithelial cells (BEAS)-2B cells and lung fibroblast CCD19 cells, suggesting a favorable therapeutic index. Mechanistic investigations demonstrated that SP09 induced G2/M cell cycle arrest in KRAS-mutant cells, as evidenced by downregulation of cyclin B1 and upregulation of p21, and activated the upstream LKB1/AMPK pathway, leading to suppression of the mTOR signaling axis and downstream effectors P70S6K, S6, and SREBP1. Collectively, these findings indicate that SP09 exerts its antitumor effects through coordinated modulation of energy-sensing and cell cycle regulatory pathways, positioning it as a promising scaffold for further drug development targeting KRAS-driven NSCLC.
Methods
Cell lines and culture
Human NSCLC cell lines A549 and H460 (KRAS G12C mutation), PC9 (EGFR delE746-A750 mutation), and the normal lung fibroblast cell lines CCD19 and BEAS-2B were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, Virginia, USA). Cells were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco, USA) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2.
Reagents
SP09 was synthesized in-house and dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, Mo, USA) to prepare a 100 mM stock solution, which was stored at −20 °C. Working concentrations were freshly prepared by diluting in culture medium, with a final DMSO concentration of ≤0.1%.
Cell viability assay
Cell viability was measured using the 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay. Briefly, cells were seeded into 96-well plates (5 × 10³ cells/well) and treated with various concentrations of SP09 (0–100 µM) for 72 h. MTT solution (5 mg/mL, Sigma-Aldrich) was added to each well and incubated for 4 h. The formazan crystals were dissolved in 100 µL DMSO, and absorbance was measured at 570 nm using a microplate reader (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA). IC50 values were calculated using GraphPad Prism 9.0.
Colony formation assay
Cells were seeded in 6-well plates (500 cells/well) and treated with SP09 for 14 days, with medium replaced every 3 days. Colonies were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min and stained with 0.1% crystal violet. Colonies containing >50 cells were counted under a microscope.
Cell cycle analysis
Cell cycle distribution was determined by flow cytometry. Cells were treated with SP09 for 24 h, harvested, washed twice with cold PBS, and fixed in 70% ethanol at 4 °C overnight. After washing, cells were incubated with RNase A (50 µg/mL) and propidium iodide (PI; 50 µg/mL; Sigma-Aldrich) for 30 min in the dark. DNA content was analyzed using a FACScan flow cytometer (BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA), and data were processed with FlowJo software.
Western blot analysis
Cells were lysed in radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Beyotime, China). Protein concentrations were determined using a BCA protein assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Equal amounts of protein (30 µg) were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membranes (Millipore, Burlington, MA, USA). After blocking with 5% nonfat milk in Tris-buffered saline with Tween-20 (TBST) for 1 h at room temperature, membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies against LKB1, phospho-LKB1 (Ser428), AMPK, phospho-AMPK (Thr172), mTOR, phospho-mTOR (Ser2448), P70S6K, phospho-P70S6K (Thr389), S6, phospho-S6 (Ser235/236), SREBP1, cyclin B1, p21, and β-actin (all from Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA). After washing, membranes were incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (CST, USA) for 1 h at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and quantified by ImageJ software, with β-actin as the loading control.
Statistical analysis
All experiments were repeated at least three times independently. Data are presented as mean ± SD. Statistical significance was determined by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test, or by Student’s t-test for two-group comparisons. A P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 8.0.
Result
SP09 selectively inhibited the growth of KRAS-mutant nonsmall cell lung cancer cells
To assess the antiproliferative activity of SP09 against NSCLC cells with distinct driver mutations, a panel of cell lines—including KRAS-mutant A549 and H460, EGFR-mutant PC9, human lung fibroblasts (CCD19), and normal human bronchial epithelial cells (BEAS-2B)—were treated with increasing concentrations of SP09 for 72 h, followed by MTT assay. The calculated IC50 values are summarized in Table 1. As shown in Figure 2a, SP09 significantly reduced the viability of all tested NSCLC cell lines in a dose-dependent manner, with IC50 values of 29.89 ± 3.66 µM (A549), 29.53 ± 5.51 µM (H460), and 18.34 ± 3.24 µM (PC9). Notably, SP09 exhibited minimal cytotoxicity toward normal lung cells (CCD19 and BEAS-2B), indicating a degree of selectivity toward malignant cells. Although PC9 cells appeared more sensitive to SP09 than KRAS-mutant A549 and H460 cells, patients harboring classical EGFR mutations can already benefit from clinically available EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. gefitinib and erlotinib) with favorable response rates. In contrast, therapeutic options for KRAS-mutant NSCLC remain limited, with only a few targeted agents available. This therapeutic gap underscores the need to explore novel compounds for KRAS-driven NSCLC. To further examine the long-term growth-suppressive effects of SP09, colony formation assays were performed in A549 and H460 cells. As shown in Figure 2b–d, SP09 treatment resulted in a concentration-dependent reduction in colony numbers. Growth suppression became evident at 10 µM in A549 cells and 20 µM in H460 cells. At 20 µM, colony numbers were reduced by approximately 50% compared with untreated controls, and at the highest tested concentration, only 5–10% of colonies remained. These findings consistently demonstrated that SP09 selectively inhibited the growth and clonogenic potential of KRAS-mutant NSCLC cells.

SP09 induced G2/M cell cycle arrest in KRAS-mutant nonsmall cell lung cancer cells
To elucidate the mechanism underlying the growth inhibition of KRAS-mutant NSCLC cells by SP09, we analyzed cell cycle distribution in A549 and H460 cells following treatment with increasing concentrations of SP09 for 24 h, using flow cytometry. As shown in Figure 3a,b, SP09 treatment resulted in a dose-dependent decrease in the proportion of cells in the G1 phase, accompanied by a marked accumulation of cells in the G2/M phase. The proportion of cells in the S phase remained unchanged, indicating that SP09 specifically induced G2/M arrest rather than a generalized cell cycle blockade. To further verify these findings, we assessed the expression of key cell cycle regulatory proteins by western blotting. As shown in Figure 3c–h, SP09 treatment for 24 h led to a dose-dependent downregulation of cyclin B1, a key regulator of G2/M transition, and upregulation of p21. This cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor enforces cell cycle arrest. These results are consistent with the flow cytometry data and collectively indicate that SP09 induced G2/M phase arrest in KRAS-mutant NSCLC cells.
SP09 inhibited proliferation of H460 cells via activation of the LKB1/AMPK pathway
To further elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying SP09-mediated growth inhibition, we selected H460 cells, a representative KRAS-mutant NSCLC line, for detailed signaling analysis. AMPK functions as a critical cellular energy sensor that regulates metabolic homeostasis and influences cell cycle progression, thereby affecting proliferation. We therefore examined the effects of SP09 on AMPK activation and its upstream and downstream signaling components. As shown in Figure 4, treatment with SP09 significantly increased phosphorylation of AMPK at Thr172 in a dose-dependent manner, without altering total AMPK protein levels, indicating activation of AMPK. The phosphorylation of Thr172 is essential for AMPK activation and is primarily mediated by the upstream serine/threonine kinase LKB1. Consistent with this mechanism, SP09 treatment also increased phosphorylation of LKB1 in H460 cells, suggesting that SP09 activates AMPK through the LKB1-dependent pathway. Given that AMPK negatively regulates mTOR signaling, we next assessed changes in mTOR pathway activity. SP09 treatment decreased phosphorylation of mTOR, indicating suppression of its activity. mTOR is a key nutrient and energy sensor that promotes protein synthesis, cell growth, and metabolism under favorable growth conditions but is inhibited upon AMPK activation. Correspondingly, phosphorylation of downstream mTOR effectors, including P70S6K and S6, as well as the expression of the lipogenic transcription factor SREBP1, was markedly reduced following SP09 treatment. SREBP1 is known to regulate lipogenesis, which is essential for cell division in both Drosophila and mammals.
In parallel, we observed that SP09 markedly enhanced the phosphorylation of AMPK and its upstream kinase LKB1, accompanied by a pronounced reduction in the phosphorylation of mTOR and its downstream effectors, including P70S6K, S6, and SREBP1. These findings suggest that SP09 activates the LKB1/AMPK axis, leading to inhibition of mTOR signaling and suppression of its downstream anabolic processes, thereby contributing to the growth-inhibitory effects observed in KRAS-mutant H460 cells.
Discussion
Targeted therapies against oncogenic drivers have been a major strategy for overcoming NSCLC. Several inhibitors are currently available and approved for patients harboring driver mutations, such as gefitinib and osimertinib for EGFR mutations, and alectinib for ALK rearrangements [6,22]. However, there are still no clinically approved inhibitors for KRAS-mutated NSCLC, making the discovery of novel agents for this subtype an urgent need in clinical oncology [23]. KRAS mutations, particularly KRAS G12C and KRAS G12D, are among the most prevalent oncogenic alterations in NSCLC, accounting for approximately 25–30% of lung adenocarcinomas in Western populations and 10–15% in Asian cohorts [24–26]. Despite the recent emergence of KRAS G12C inhibitors, resistance typically develops within months via secondary KRAS mutations or bypass signaling activation, underscoring the need for alternative strategies that target broader KRAS-mutant contexts beyond a single allele [23,27].
In recent years, natural products and their derivatives have attracted increasing attention as potential sources for anticancer drug discovery [28,29]. In the present study, we report for the first time that SP09, a synthetic derivative of benzoin, exerts potent inhibitory effects against KRAS-mutant NSCLC cells, while showing low cytotoxicity toward normal lung epithelial and fibroblast cells.
Our results demonstrated that SP09 markedly suppressed the proliferation of NSCLC cells with KRAS and EGFR mutations, with particularly strong effects observed in PC9, A549, and H460 cells. Consistent with MTT assay results, colony formation assays further confirmed that SP09 significantly reduced the clonogenic ability of KRAS-mutant A549 and H460 cells. Morphologically, SP09-treated cells exhibited notable changes within 24 h, including an oblate shape and cell membrane shrinkage, indicating cellular stress or cytoskeletal alterations. These antiproliferative effects were closely associated with cell cycle modulation [30,31].
Cell cycle dysregulation is a hallmark of NSCLC progression [32]. Flow cytometry analysis revealed that SP09 treatment significantly increased the proportion of cells in the G2/M phase while reducing the G1-phase population in A549 and H460 cells, suggesting G2/M phase arrest. Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) orchestrate the cell cycle by forming complexes with cyclins at specific phases [33]. In G2/M progression, the cyclinA-CDK1 and cyclinB-CDK1 complexes ensure correct mitotic entry, while the CDK inhibitor p21 suppresses cyclinB-CDK1 activity [34,35]. In our study, SP09 treatment led to upregulation of p21 and downregulation of cyclin B1, indicating that G2/M arrest was mediated, at least in part, by p21-dependent suppression of cyclin B1 expression.
Beyond direct effects on cell cycle regulators, our data suggest that SP09 modulates upstream signaling pathways controlling proliferation and metabolism. The AMPK pathway plays a pivotal role in coordinating energy homeostasis and cell cycle progression [36–38]. Western blotting revealed that SP09 robustly increased AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172 without altering total AMPK levels. This activation was accompanied by elevated phosphorylation of its upstream kinase LKB1. Furthermore, SP09 treatment reduced phosphorylation of mTOR and its downstream effectors p70S6K and S6, as well as the lipogenic transcription factor SREBP1. In parallel, phosphorylation AMPK target involved in lipid metabolism was increased. These findings indicate that SP09 activates the LKB1/AMPK axis while inhibiting mTOR signaling, thereby impairing anabolic processes essential for NSCLC cell growth and potentially contributing to the observed G2/M phase arrest.
In summary, our study identifies SP09 as a novel benzoin-Schiff base derivative that effectively suppresses the proliferation of KRAS-mutant NSCLC cells through dual mechanisms: induction of G2/M phase arrest and modulation of the LKB1/AMPK/mTOR signaling pathway (Fig. 5). These findings provide experimental evidence supporting SP09 as a promising candidate for further preclinical evaluation in KRAS-driven NSCLC.
Conclusion
In this study, we demonstrated that SP09 selectively inhibited the proliferation of NSCLC cells, with notable activity against KRAS-mutant subtypes, while exhibiting minimal cytotoxicity toward normal lung epithelial and fibroblast cells. MTT and colony formation assays confirmed that SP09 reduced the viability and clonogenic potential of A549 and H460 cells in a concentration-dependent manner.
Mechanistic investigations revealed that SP09 induced G2/M phase cell cycle arrest in KRAS-mutant NSCLC cells, as evidenced by flow cytometry analysis and associated with downregulation of cyclin B1 and upregulation of p21. Furthermore, SP09 activated the LKB1/AMPK signaling cascade, as indicated by increased phosphorylation of LKB1 and AMPK at Thr172, without altering total AMPK levels. This activation led to suppression of the mTOR pathway, reflected by decreased phosphorylation of mTOR and its downstream effectors P70S6K, S6, and SREBP1. Collectively, these data indicate that SP09 exerts its antiproliferative effects by simultaneously disrupting cell cycle progression and inhibiting anabolic metabolism through modulation of the LKB1/AMPK/mTOR axis.
